claim: RIM-BP2 is expressed in the whole hippocampal neuropil, with strong labeling of the mossy-fiber layer band in the CA3 stratum lucidum.
source: Immunostainings for RIM-BP2 in mouse hippocampal slices revealed RIM-BP2 expression in the whole hippocampal neuropil, with a strong labeling of the mossy-fiber layer band in the CA3 stratum lucidum (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1a and described in the text.

claim: The ratio of fEPSP to presynaptic fiber volley (PFV) is drastically reduced at MF synapses in RIM-BP2 deficient slices compared to WT slices.
source: The ratio of fEPSP to presynaptic fiber volley (PFV) was drastically reduced when stimulating the MF pathway in RIM-BP2 deficient (KO) slices compared to that in WT slices (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Neurotransmission is severely impaired upon loss of RIM-BP2 at MF synapses.
source: This shows that neurotransmission is severely impaired upon loss of RIM-BP2 at MF synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the drastic reduction in fEPSP/PFV ratio at MF synapses in RIM-BP2 KO mice.

claim: The ratio of fEPSP to PFV for associative commissural (AC)-fibers and Schaffer collaterals (SC) is not affected by the loss of RIM-BP2.
source: In contrast, the ratio of fEPSP to presynaptic fiber volley (PFV) for associative commissural (AC)-fibers and Schaffer collaterals (SC), both representing small central synapses, were not affected by the loss of RIM-BP2 (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: RIM-BP2 deletion specifically impairs neurotransmitter release at hippocampal MF synapses, compared to AC and SC synapses.
source: Thus, RIM-BP2 deletion specifically impairs neurotransmitter release at hippocampal MF synapses, compared to AC and SC synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of RIM-BP2 deletion on fEPSP/PFV ratios at different synapse types.

claim: Normalized fEPSP amplitudes are significantly increased in RIM-BP2 deficient synapses at the end of 1 Hz train stimulation.
source: Normalized fEPSPs amplitudes were significantly increased in RIM-BP2 deficient synapses at the end of 1 Hz train stimulation, suggesting a role of RIM-BP2 in short-term plasticity at the MF synapse (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by frequency facilitation experiments shown in Figure 1d.

claim: RIM-BP2 plays a role in short-term plasticity at the MF synapse.
source: Normalized fEPSPs amplitudes were significantly increased in RIM-BP2 deficient synapses at the end of 1 Hz train stimulation, suggesting a role of RIM-BP2 in short-term plasticity at the MF synapse (Figure 1d).
evidence: Inferred from the increased facilitation observed in RIM-BP2 KO synapses during 1 Hz stimulation.

claim: The average distance of the closest RIM-BP2 cluster relative to a given Bassoon cluster at MF synapses is comparable to CA3-CA1 synapses.
source: The average distance of the closest RIM-BP2 cluster relative to a given Bassoon cluster at MF synapses was comparable to CA3-CA1 synapses.
evidence: Based on gSTED microscopy analysis comparing protein cluster distances between synapse types.

claim: The closest Munc13-1 cluster in the MF synapse is 51% further away from a RIM-BP2 cluster (174 ± 20 nm) than at CA3-CA1 synapses (115 ± 5 nm).
source: However, the closest Munc13-1 cluster in the MF synapse was 51% further away from a RIM-BP2 cluster (174 ± 20 nm, Figure 2c) than what we previously observed at CA3-CA1 synapses (115 ± 5 nm) (Grauel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy measurements and comparison with previously published data from Grauel et al., 2016.

claim: At WT MF boutons, there are at least three Munc13-1 clusters, two Bassoon clusters and four RIM-BP2 clusters within a single active zone.
source: Based on ultrastructural studies of MF AZ size, estimating an AZ diameter of 391 nm, at WT MFBs we detected at least three Munc13-1 clusters, two Bassoon clusters and four RIM-BP2 clusters within a single AZ, having a dk <391 nm.
evidence: Based on gSTED analysis combined with ultrastructural data on MF active zone size from Rollenhagen et al., 2007.

claim: The loss of RIM-BP2 does not alter the number, ratio, or distance of RIM1 or Homer1 clusters to a given Cav2.1 cluster at MF synapses.
source: Surprisingly, neither the number, the ratio of protein clusters nor the distance of RIM1 or Homer1 clusters to a given Cav2.1 cluster were altered upon the loss of RIM-BP2 (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy analysis shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: At WT MF boutons, there are three Cav2.1 clusters and one RIM1 cluster per single active zone.
source: Based on ultrastructural studies of MF AZ size, estimating an AZ diameter of 391 nm, at WT MFBs we detected one RIM1 cluster and three Cav2.1 clusters per single active zone, having a dk <391 nm.
evidence: Based on gSTED analysis combined with ultrastructural data on MF active zone size.

claim: The cluster number of RIM1 and the nearest neighbor distance between Homer1 and RIM1 clusters are unaltered in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses.
source: The cluster number of RIM1 as well as the nearest neighbor distance between Homer1 and RIM1 clusters was unaltered in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses (Figure 2g,h).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy analysis shown in Figure 2g,h.

claim: The loss of RIM-BP2 does not grossly alter RIM1 cluster number or localization at MF terminals.
source: Although we observed a higher variability in the RIM1/Cav2.1 cluster ratio in RIM-BP2 KO mice (Figure 2e,f), our data suggest that the loss of RIM-BP2 does not grossly alter RIM1 cluster number or localization at MF terminals.
evidence: Based on gSTED microscopy analysis of RIM1 and Cav2.1 clusters.

claim: The distance between RIM1 and Cav2.1 clusters in MF synapses is 35% larger than in CA3-CA1 synapses.
source: Interestingly, we found a 35% larger distance between RIM1 and Cav2.1 in MF synapses, again suggesting a differential nanoarchitecture of MF active zones.
evidence: Based on comparison of gSTED data from MF and CA3-CA1 synapses acquired from the same brain slices.

claim: There is a drastic reduction in the number of Munc13-1 clusters in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses.
source: Interestingly, we found a drastic reduction in the number of Munc13-1 clusters in RIM-BP2 deficient synapses, accompanied by a decrease in Munc13-1 clusters at specific distances from a given Cav2.1 clusters (Figure 3a–e).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3a-e.

claim: In RIM-BP2 deficient MF active zones, Munc13-1 clusters are located at an increased distance to Cav2.1 clusters compared to WT MF synapses.
source: Therefore, in RIM-BP2 deficient MF active zones we detect less Munc13-1 clusters, which also were located at an increased distance to Cav2.1 clusters compared to WT MF synapses (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: The Munc13-1 cluster number and distribution at CA3-CA1 synapses are unaltered upon RIM-BP2 loss.
source: In contrast, the Munc13-1 cluster number and distribution at CA3-CA1 synapses were unaltered upon RIM-BP2 loss (Figure 3h–m), indicating that the observed reduction in the Munc13-1 cluster number is specific for MF synapses.
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3h-m.

claim: The reduction in Munc13-1 cluster number upon RIM-BP2 loss is specific for MF synapses.
source: In contrast, the Munc13-1 cluster number and distribution at CA3-CA1 synapses were unaltered upon RIM-BP2 loss (Figure 3h–m), indicating that the observed reduction in the Munc13-1 cluster number is specific for MF synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of RIM-BP2 deletion on Munc13-1 clusters at MF versus CA3-CA1 synapses.

claim: Peak-to-peak distance measurements reveal a significantly increased distance of Munc13-1 clusters relative to Cav2.1 clusters in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses compared to WT.
source: Peak-to-peak distance measurements revealed a significantly increased distance of Munc13-1 clusters relative to Cav2.1 clusters in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses compared to WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting our results from the semi-automated k nearest neighbor analysis.
evidence: Supported by line profile measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RIM-BP2 is essential in stabilizing Munc13-1 protein clusters specifically at MF synapses.
source: Altogether, our gSTED analysis demonstrates that RIM-BP2 is essential in stabilizing Munc13-1 protein clusters specifically at MF synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the drastic reduction in Munc13-1 clusters at MF but not CA3-CA1 synapses upon RIM-BP2 deletion.

claim: Deletion of RIM-BP2 results in a significant reduction of Munc13-1 intensity levels at MF synapses but not at CA3-CA1 terminals.
source: Deletion of RIM-BP2 resulted in a significant reduction of Munc13-1 intensity levels at MF synapses but not at CA3-CA1 terminals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of RIM-BP2 neither alters the number of protein clusters nor the distribution of Munc13-2 clusters relative to Cav2.1 channels at both MF and CA3-CA1 synapses.
source: In both synapses, loss of RIM-BP2 neither altered the number of protein clusters nor the distribution of Munc13-2 clusters relative to Cav2.1 channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), showing that the observed electrophysiological phenotype is not due to Munc13-2 loss (Breustedt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and citation to Breustedt et al., 2010.

claim: The observed electrophysiological phenotype is not due to Munc13-2 loss.
source: In both synapses, loss of RIM-BP2 neither altered the number of protein clusters nor the distribution of Munc13-2 clusters relative to Cav2.1 channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), showing that the observed electrophysiological phenotype is not due to Munc13-2 loss (Breustedt et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of change in Munc13-2 clusters upon RIM-BP2 deletion, combined with citation to Breustedt et al., 2010.

claim: There is a ~25% reduction in docked synaptic vesicles in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses compared to WT MF synapses.
source: High-pressure freezing of acute hippocampal slices (4–6 weeks) show a ~ 25% reduction in docked SVs in RIM-BP2 deficient MF synapses compared to WT MF synapses (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The size of the post-synaptic density (PSD) is unaltered upon the loss of RIM-BP2 at MF synapses.
source: The size of the post-synaptic density (PSD) was unaltered upon the loss of RIM-BP2 indicating that RIM-BP2 does not affect trans-synaptic interactions at MF synapses (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: RIM-BP2 does not affect trans-synaptic interactions at MF synapses.
source: The size of the post-synaptic density (PSD) was unaltered upon the loss of RIM-BP2 indicating that RIM-BP2 does not affect trans-synaptic interactions at MF synapses (Figure 4b).
evidence: Inferred from the unchanged PSD size in RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses.

claim: The number of docked synaptic vesicles in CA1 synapses is unaltered in RIM-BP2 deficient synapses compared to synapses from WT slices.
source: However as expected from previous results in culture (Grauel et al., 2016), the number of docked SVs in CA1 synapses was unaltered in RIM-BP2 deficient synapses compared to synapses from WT slices (Figure 4b,f).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4b,f and citation to Grauel et al., 2016.

claim: The number of large docked vesicles per active zone is not affected by the deletion of RIM-BP2 at MF synapses.
source: The number of large docked vesicles per active zone was however not affected by the deletion of RIM-BP2 (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: In contrast to CA3-CA1 synapses, MF synapses require RIM-BP2 dependent stabilization of Munc13-1 at the active zone to dock synaptic vesicles.
source: Thus, in contrast to CA3-CA1 synapses, MF synapses require RIM-BP2 dependent stabilization of Munc13-1 at the active zone to dock synaptic vesicles.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of RIM-BP2 deletion on vesicle docking at MF versus CA3-CA1 synapses.

claim: Cultured granule cells form MF-like boutons as assessed by EM analysis.
source: It is important to note that cultured granule cells form MF like boutons as assessed by EM analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and are sensitive to the application of DCG IV (Figure 5a,b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy and pharmacological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5a,b.

claim: Cultured granule cells are sensitive to the application of DCG IV.
source: It is important to note that cultured granule cells form MF like boutons as assessed by EM analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and are sensitive to the application of DCG IV (Figure 5a,b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5a,b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Granule autaptic neurons exhibit key aspects of hippocampal granule cell identity.
source: Therefore, granule autaptic neurons exhibit key aspects of hippocampal granule cell identity.
evidence: Inferred from the MF-like bouton morphology and DCG IV sensitivity of cultured granule cells.

claim: Evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) are severely impaired in RIM-BP2 KO granule cell autapses compared to WT autapses.
source: Consistent with the findings from hippocampal field recordings (Figure 1), evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) were severely impaired in RIM-BP2 KO granule cell autapses as compared to that in WT autapses (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Rescue of RIM-BP2 deficiency by lentiviral expression in RIM-BP2 KO neurons completely restores synaptic transmission.
source: Rescue of RIM-BP2 deficiency by lentiviral expression in RIM-BP2 KO neurons completely restored synaptic transmission, confirming the specificity of RIM-BP2 function at these synapses (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: The size of the readily releasable pool (RRP) is significantly reduced in RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses.
source: In line with the finding that RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses had only half the number of docked vesicles compared to that in WT neurons (Figure 4), the size of the RRP was significantly reduced (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: Supported by hypertonic sucrose application experiments shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: The frequency and amplitude of Ca2+-independent release events (mEPSCs) are not significantly altered upon RIM-BP2 loss in granule autapses.
source: The frequency and amplitude of Ca2+-independent release events as measured by recording spontaneous miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) were not significantly altered upon RIM-BP2 loss (Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by mEPSC recordings shown in Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Vesicular release probability (Pvr) is not significantly different between RIM-BP2 KO and WT granule autapses.
source: We next assessed vesicular release probability Pvr, as the ratio of EPSC and RRP charge, and RIM-BP2 KO and WT granule autapses were not significantly different (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by Pvr calculations shown in Figure 5d.

claim: RIM-BP2 KO neurons display enhanced facilitation compared to WT neurons at 25 ms interstimulus interval.
source: However, utilizing paired-pulse ratio (PPR, 25 ms interstimulus interval), we found that RIM-BP2 KO neurons displayed enhanced facilitation compared to WT neurons, which could be rescued by re-expression of RIM-BP2 (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: Supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments shown in Figure 5e,f.

claim: At all but one interstimulus intervals tested (250 ms), paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) is increased in RIM-BP2 KO granule autapses.
source: At all but one interstimulus intervals tested (250 ms), PPF was increased (Figure 5g).
evidence: Supported by paired-pulse ratio experiments with varying interstimulus intervals shown in Figure 5g.

claim: EPSCs evoked by 10 Hz action potential trains display less depression over the 5 s train duration in RIM-BP2 KO granule cell autapses compared to WT or rescue groups.
source: Also, EPSCs evoked by 10 Hz action potential trains displayed less depression over the 5 s train duration in RIM-BP2 KO granule cell autapses compared to WT or rescue groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: Supported by 10 Hz train stimulation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b,c.

claim: Loss of RIM-BP2 leads to impaired hippocampal granule cell output due to changes in both vesicle docking/priming and release during repeated stimuli.
source: Thus, loss of RIM-BP2 leads to impaired hippocampal granule cell output, due to changes in both vesicle docking/priming and due to changes in release during repeated stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects on RRP size and short-term plasticity in RIM-BP2 KO granule autapses.

claim: Munc13-1 K32E expression in RIM-BP2 KO granule neurons is sufficient to rescue the RRP.
source: Remarkably, Munc13-1 K32E expression in RIM-BP2 KO granule neurons sufficed to rescue the RRP, whereas Munc13-1 WT was not sufficient to rescue vesicle priming upon RIM-BP2 deletion (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with Munc13-1 mutants shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Munc13-1 WT is not sufficient to rescue vesicle priming upon RIM-BP2 deletion in granule autapses.
source: Remarkably, Munc13-1 K32E expression in RIM-BP2 KO granule neurons sufficed to rescue the RRP, whereas Munc13-1 WT was not sufficient to rescue vesicle priming upon RIM-BP2 deletion (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with Munc13-1 mutants shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Evoked release can be rescued by Munc13-1 K32E but not by Munc13-1 WT in RIM-BP2 KO granule autapses.
source: In line with the RRP, evoked release could not be rescued by Munc13-1 WT, but required the constitutive active form of Munc13-1 K32E (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with Munc13-1 mutants shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Pvr is neither altered upon RIM-BP2 deletion nor by the rescue of Munc13-1 WT or Munc13-1 K32E in granule autapses.
source: Again, the Pvr was neither altered upon RIM-BP2 deletion nor by the rescue of Munc13-1 WT or Munc13-1 K32E (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by Pvr calculations in rescue experiments shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In MF synapses, the recruitment or stabilization of active monomeric Munc13-1 is RIM-BP2 dependent.
source: These results suggest that in MF synapses, unlike hippocampal pyramidal neuron synapses, the recruitment or stabilization of active monomeric Munc13-1 is RIM-BP2 dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of RRP and evoked release by Munc13-1 K32E but not WT in RIM-BP2 KO granule autapses.

claim: Functional synaptic diversity has been found to be critical for routing and encoding sensory information within networks of neurons in the brain.
source: In recent years, functional synaptic diversity has been found to be critical for routing and encoding sensory information within networks of neurons in the brain (Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: Functional synaptic diversity has been observed both within and across brain regions.
source: Functional synaptic diversity has been observed both within and across brain regions, and it has been shown to play a significant role in temporal coding of multisensory integration and extraction of specific sensory features (Atwood and Karunanithi, 2002; O'Rourke et al., 2012; Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atwood and Karunanithi, 2002; O'Rourke et al., 2012; Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: The molecular origin of synaptic heterogeneity is largely unknown.
source: Still, the molecular origin of this heterogeneity is largely unknown, and analyses of genotype-phenotype differences across species and brain tissue have just started to uncover key molecular principles responsible for synaptic diversity, emphasizing the importance of abundance and isoforms differences across species for synaptic diversity (Rosenmund et al., 2002; Weston et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013; Böhme et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rosenmund et al., 2002; Weston et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2013; Böhme et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of RIM-BPs manifests in severe phenotypes in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ).
source: Here, RIM-binding proteins (RIM-BPs) are particularly interesting, as their loss manifests in severe phenotypes in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ) (Liu et al., 2011), but rather subtle phenotypes in small central murine synapses, the Calyx of Held or the ribbon synapse with only mild impairments in Ca2+-channel-release site coupling (Acuna et al., 2015; Grauel et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2017; Davydova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of RIM-BPs results in rather subtle phenotypes in small central murine synapses, the Calyx of Held or the ribbon synapse with only mild impairments in Ca2+-channel-release site coupling.
source: Here, RIM-binding proteins (RIM-BPs) are particularly interesting, as their loss manifests in severe phenotypes in the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ) (Liu et al., 2011), but rather subtle phenotypes in small central murine synapses, the Calyx of Held or the ribbon synapse with only mild impairments in Ca2+-channel-release site coupling (Acuna et al., 2015; Grauel et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2017; Davydova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Acuna et al., 2015; Grauel et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2017; Davydova et al., 2014.

claim: At hippocampal pyramidal CA3-CA1 synapses, RIM-BP2 loss has a mild effect on neurotransmitter release by only regulating Ca2+-secretion coupling.
source: At hippocampal pyramidal CA3-CA1 synapses, RIM-BP2 loss has a mild effect on neurotransmitter release, by only regulating Ca2+-secretion coupling.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a summary of findings.

claim: At hippocampal mossy fiber synapses, RIM-BP2 has a substantial impact on neurotransmitter release by promoting vesicle docking/priming and vesicular release probability via stabilization of Munc13-1 at the active zone.
source: However, at hippocampal mossy fiber synapses, RIM-BP2 has a substantial impact on neurotransmitter release by promoting vesicle docking/priming and vesicular release probability via stabilization of Munc13-1 at the active zone.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a summary of findings.

claim: Differences in the active zone organization may dictate the role a protein plays in synaptic transmission.
source: We suggest that differences in the active zone organization may dictate the role a protein plays in synaptic transmission and that differences in active zone architecture is a major determinant factor in the functional diversity of synapses.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claim: Differences in active zone architecture is a major determinant factor in the functional diversity of synapses.
source: We suggest that differences in the active zone organization may dictate the role a protein plays in synaptic transmission and that differences in active zone architecture is a major determinant factor in the functional diversity of synapses.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claim: At SC synapses RIM-BP2 maintains high fidelity coupling of Ca2+-channels to release sites.
source: While at SC synapses RIM-BP2 maintains high fidelity coupling of Ca2+-channels to release sites, at MF synapses RIM-BP2 is required to stabilize Munc13-1 clusters to ensure vesicle docking/priming.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings comparing SC and MF synapses.

claim: At MF synapses RIM-BP2 is required to stabilize Munc13-1 clusters to ensure vesicle docking/priming.
source: While at SC synapses RIM-BP2 maintains high fidelity coupling of Ca2+-channels to release sites, at MF synapses RIM-BP2 is required to stabilize Munc13-1 clusters to ensure vesicle docking/priming.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings comparing SC and MF synapses.

claim: RIM-BP2 deletion alters vesicular release probability at MF terminals most probably via increased distances between Ca2+-channels and release sites mapped by Munc13-1.
source: In addition, RIM-BP2 deletion alters vesicular release probability at MF terminals most probably via increased distances between Ca2+-channels and release sites mapped by Munc13-1.
evidence: Proposed as an explanation for the observed changes in release probability.

claim: RIM-BP2 and Munc13-1 clusters as well as RIM1 and Cav2.1 clusters are positioned at increased distances in MF synapses compared to CA3-CA1 synapses.
source: Finally, our analysis of the active zone architecture revealed that RIM-BP2 and Munc13-1 clusters as well as RIM1 and Cav2.1 clusters are positioned at increased distances in MF synapses compared to that in CA3-CA1 synapses, demonstrating that these synapses utilize different architectural organizational principles.
evidence: Based on gSTED microscopy analysis comparing protein cluster distances between synapse types.

claim: MF and CA3-CA1 synapses utilize different architectural organizational principles.
source: Finally, our analysis of the active zone architecture revealed that RIM-BP2 and Munc13-1 clusters as well as RIM1 and Cav2.1 clusters are positioned at increased distances in MF synapses compared to that in CA3-CA1 synapses, demonstrating that these synapses utilize different architectural organizational principles.
evidence: Inferred from the differential positioning of protein clusters at MF versus CA3-CA1 synapses.

claim: At MF synapses RIM-BP2 acts first to stabilize RIM1/Munc13-1 at the active zone, whereas at SC synapses, RIM-BP2 impacts synaptic function following RIM/Munc13-1 priming of SV vesicles at the active zone.
source: At MF synapses RIM-BP2 acts first to stabilize RIM1/Munc13-1 at the active zone, whereas at SC synapses, RIM-BP2 impacts synaptic function following RIM/Munc13-1 priming of SV vesicles at the active zone.
evidence: Proposed as an explanation for the differential functional hierarchy of RIM-BP2 at different synapse types.

claim: RIM-BP2 dependent stabilization of Munc13-1 still requires RIM activity.
source: However, RIM-BP2 dependent stabilization of Munc13-1 still requires RIM activity, since Munc13-1 K32E, the constitutively active form of Munc13-1, but not Munc13-1 WT, is sufficient to rescue the RIM-BP2 MF phenotype (Figure 6; and Deng et al., 2011; Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments with Munc13-1 mutants and supported by citations to Deng et al., 2011; Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006.

claim: The reduction in release probability at MF synapses might be due to the pronounced function of Munc13-2 in RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses.
source: Also, the reduction in release probability might be due to the pronounced function of Munc13-2 in RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses (Rosenmund et al., 2002), since Munc13-1 clusters but not Munc13-2 clusters abundance and localization are altered upon RIM-BP2 deletion.
evidence: Proposed as an alternative explanation for the observed changes in release probability, supported by citation to Rosenmund et al., 2002.

claim: In mammalian synapses and Drosophila NMJ, RIM-BPs have been shown to biochemically interact with Ca2+-channels.
source: In mammalian synapses and Drosophila NMJ, RIM-BPs have been shown to biochemically interact with Ca2+-channels (Liu et al., 2011; Davydova et al., 2014), resulting in a severe loss of overall Ca2+-channel densities at RIM-BP deficient NMJ's (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2011; Davydova et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of RIM-BPs results in a severe loss of overall Ca2+-channel densities at RIM-BP deficient Drosophila NMJs.
source: In mammalian synapses and Drosophila NMJ, RIM-BPs have been shown to biochemically interact with Ca2+-channels (Liu et al., 2011; Davydova et al., 2014), resulting in a severe loss of overall Ca2+-channel densities at RIM-BP deficient NMJ's (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: Central mammalian synapses show no discernable signs of Ca2+-channel dysfunction upon RIM-BP loss, but just moderate to weak changes in synaptic transmission, compatible with an impaired Ca2+-secretion coupling mechanism.
source: In contrast, central mammalian synapses show no discernable signs of Ca2+-channel dysfunction, but just moderate to weak changes in synaptic transmission, compatible with an impaired Ca2+-secretion coupling mechanism (Grauel et al., 2016; Davydova et al., 2014; Acuna et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grauel et al., 2016; Davydova et al., 2014; Acuna et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of RIM-BP2 causes changes in short term plasticity properties, indicative of a role of RIM-BP2 in regulating release probability and short-term plasticity.
source: However, the effect is sufficiently strong to cause changes in short term plasticity properties, indicative of a role of RIM-BP2 in regulating release probability and short-term plasticity, similar to what has been observed by loss of the four mammalian rab3 genes (Schlüter et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in short-term plasticity and supported by citation to Schlüter et al., 2006.

claim: Munc13-1 is essential for neurotransmitter release in a variety of synapses.
source: Some highly conserved proteins, like Munc13-1, are essential for neurotransmitter release in a variety of synapses, since they exclusively conduct one specific function, in this case vesicle docking and priming (Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Weimer et al., 2006; Aravamudan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Weimer et al., 2006; Aravamudan et al., 1999.

claim: Munc13-1 exclusively conducts vesicle docking and priming.
source: Some highly conserved proteins, like Munc13-1, are essential for neurotransmitter release in a variety of synapses, since they exclusively conduct one specific function, in this case vesicle docking and priming (Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Weimer et al., 2006; Aravamudan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Augustin et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Weimer et al., 2006; Aravamudan et al., 1999.

claim: RIM-BP2 function depends on the synapse type where it is expressed.
source: Therefore, RIM-BP2 function depends on the synapse type where it is expressed.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phenotypes of RIM-BP2 loss at different synapse types.

claim: Differences in the structural organization of active zones might be responsible for the observed phenotypes of RIM-BP2 loss at different synapse types.
source: We propose that differences in the structural organization of active zones might be responsible for the observed phenotypes.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis to explain the differential effects of RIM-BP2 loss.

claim: A single active zone may contain more than one protein cluster of key active zone proteins.
source: Therefore, our STED analysis suggests that a single active zone may contain more than one protein cluster of key active zone proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the gSTED analysis showing multiple clusters within estimated active zone dimensions.

claim: The distance measurements between clusters of vesicle docking/priming factor Munc13-1 and Ca2+-channels at MF terminals are in the same range as previously reported in the NMJ and CNS of Drosophila.
source: However, the distance measurements between clusters of vesicle docking/priming factor Munc13-1 and Ca2+-channels we retrieved at MF terminals were in the same range of what was previously reported in the NMJ and CNS of Drosophila (Fulterer et al., 2018), and were also similar to estimates for Ca2+-secretion coupling distances from physiological recordings using efficacy tests of slow Ca2+-chelators (Aravamudan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by comparison with data from Fulterer et al., 2018 and Aravamudan et al., 1999.

claim: Loss of RIM-BP2 leads to an overall reduction in Munc13-1 levels at MF synapses.
source: In confocal fluorescence measurements performed in parallel to gSTED imaging, we observed that loss of RIM-BP2 led to an overall reduction in Munc13-1 levels at MF synapses.
evidence: Supported by confocal fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: Loss of RIM-BP2 does not alter overall Munc13-1 levels at SC synapses.
source: This is in contrast to SC synapses and overall unchanged Munc13-1 levels by western analysis on synaptosomal fraction (Grauel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grauel et al., 2016.

claim: RIM-BP2 has a specific role in stabilizing Munc13-1 at active zones of MF synapses and consequently the establishment of Munc13-1 clusters.
source: These combined results argue for a specific role of RIM-BP2 in stabilizing Munc13-1 at active zones of MF synapses and consequently the establishment of Munc13-1 clusters.
evidence: Inferred from the combined gSTED and confocal fluorescence data showing reduced Munc13-1 clusters and overall levels at MF synapses.

claim: At SC synapses, vesicle priming is accomplished by the interaction of RIM1 and Munc13-1 independent of RIM-BP2.
source: This effect could be indirect via RIM, as it is known for SC synapses where vesicle priming is accomplished by the interaction of RIM1 and Munc13-1 independent of RIM-BP2 (Deng et al., 2011; Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006), or perhaps through direct interactions via RIM-BP2, as previously shown in Drosophila (Böhme et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deng et al., 2011; Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006.

claim: RIM-BP2 may interact directly with Munc13-1, as previously shown in Drosophila.
source: This effect could be indirect via RIM, as it is known for SC synapses where vesicle priming is accomplished by the interaction of RIM1 and Munc13-1 independent of RIM-BP2 (Deng et al., 2011; Andrews-Zwilling et al., 2006), or perhaps through direct interactions via RIM-BP2, as previously shown in Drosophila (Böhme et al., 2016).
evidence: Proposed as a possible mechanism, supported by citation to Böhme et al., 2016.

claim: A critical role of RIM-BP2 in Munc13 recruitment is consistent with the docking/priming phenotype of RIM-BP2 loss in the fly NMJ where the reduction in Munc13 levels is severe upon loss of RIM-BP.
source: A critical role of RIM-BP2 in Munc13 recruitment is consistent with the docking/priming phenotype of RIM-BP2 loss in the fly NMJ where the reduction in Munc13 levels is severe upon loss of RIM-BP (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: The electron micrographs from RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses revealed a 25% loss of docked vesicles, similar to what has been previously shown for Munc13-1/−2 deficient central synapses.
source: The electron micrographs from RIM-BP2 KO MF synapses revealed in addition to a 25% loss of docked vesicles, similarly to what has been previously shown for Munc13-1/−2 deficient central synapses (Imig et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data and citation to Imig et al., 2014.

claim: The MF synapse is more sensitive to reductions in Munc13-1 levels, leading to stronger impairment in forming functional Munc13-1 clusters.
source: Putting this together with the gSTED analysis, we speculate that the MF synapse is more sensitive to reductions in Munc13-1 levels, leading to stronger impairment in forming functional Munc13-1 clusters.
evidence: Proposed as a speculation based on the combined EM and gSTED data.

claim: RIM is less expressed in the MF synapses compared to SC synapses.
source: For example, RIM, a critical interaction partner of Munc13-1, is less expressed in the MF synapses compared to SC synapses (Cembrowski et al., 2016), and therefore loss of RIM-BP2 cannot be redundantly supported by RIM-Munc13 interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cembrowski et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of RIM-BP2 at MF synapses cannot be redundantly supported by RIM-Munc13 interactions due to lower RIM expression.
source: For example, RIM, a critical interaction partner of Munc13-1, is less expressed in the MF synapses compared to SC synapses (Cembrowski et al., 2016), and therefore loss of RIM-BP2 cannot be redundantly supported by RIM-Munc13 interactions.
evidence: Proposed as an explanation for the differential sensitivity to RIM-BP2 loss, supported by citation to Cembrowski et al., 2016.

claim: The functional hierarchy of the triple complex formed by RIM-BP2/RIM1/Munc13-1 is fundamentally different between SC and MF synapses.
source: In any case, the functional hierarchy of the triple complex formed by RIM-BP2/RIM1/Munc13-1 appears fundamentally different between SC and MF synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of RIM-BP2 loss on vesicle priming and Munc13-1 stabilization at different synapse types.

claim: Relative Ca2+-channel localization at the MF synapses is not affected by the deletion of RIM-BP2.
source: Interestingly, relative Ca2+-channel localization at the MF synapses is not affected by the deletion of RIM-BP2, therefore the changes in release probability are rather due to increased coupling distances between Ca2+-channels and Munc13-1 as previously shown in C. elegans (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by gSTED microscopy data showing unchanged Cav2.1 localization.
